prompt: The shop's plan is a `P1v3` with two instances. The developers put their small admin site on the same plan. What happens to what the plan costs?
hint: Ask what the bill on a dedicated tier is counted in.

choices.text: A third instance is added for the admin site
choices.why: An app brings no machines with it; it runs on the plan's instances, which stay at two.

choices.text: Nothing: the admin site runs on the same two instances
choices.why: On a dedicated tier each instance is charged, whatever and however much runs on it; the cost of the second app is the capacity it takes.

choices.text: The admin site is charged per request on top of the plan
choices.why: There is no per-request charge on an App Service plan; that is closer to the Consumption profile of lesson 8.

choices.text: It doubles, because each app is charged for the instances it runs on
choices.why: That would be true if apps were billed; it is the instances that are, once each.

prompt: A copy of the shop's file loses the line `reserved: true` and compiles with no warning. What has changed in what Azure would build?
hint: The compiler checked types. Read what the REST API says the property means, and its default.

choices.text: Nothing, because `kind: 'linux'` already makes the plan a Linux one
choices.why: The plan's operating system is decided by `reserved`; `kind` on its own does not make the plan Linux.

choices.text: Nothing that matters, or the compiler would have warned
choices.why: The compiler warns about types and names. A property left out that has a default is a valid file that means something else.

choices.text: The plan would be a Windows plan, since `reserved` defaults to false
choices.why: The REST API describes `reserved` as true for a Linux plan and false otherwise, with false as its default.

choices.text: The plan stays Linux, and the site switches to a built-in Python runtime
choices.why: Nothing in the file asks for a built-in runtime; the image is still named in `linuxFxVersion`, and the plan is the part that changed.

prompt: A plan of three instances carries two apps, and one of them has a staging slot. Per-app scaling is off. How many app copies, slots included, are running across the plan's instances?
hint: A slot is an app on the same machines, and every app runs on every instance.

prompt: On Linux, the shop's site names its image as `linuxFxVersion: '___|shopregistry.azurecr.io/shop:1.0'`.
hint: The word in front of the vertical bar names the kind of thing the string describes.

prompt: Which of these is true of the app setting `WEBSITES_PORT` in the shop's file?
hint: Two of Microsoft's pages describe the default differently, and one of them says where the setting goes.

choices.text: It is how the shop's code learns which port to listen on
choices.why: The setting is read by the platform and is not passed to the container; the shop reads `PORT`, set in its Dockerfile.

choices.text: It opens a second port beside 80, so the shop answers on both
choices.why: App Service sends HTTP to one port of a container; the setting says which one, and adds none.

choices.text: It is the port the health check uses to reach `/healthz`
choices.why: The health check asks a path on the app; the port the platform routes to is the same for every request.

choices.text: It states 8080 so the file does not rely on port detection
choices.why: One page says App Service tries 80 and 8080, another that it assumes 80; naming the port removes the question.

prompt: `SHOP_ENV` decides whether the shop calls the real payment gateway or its sandbox. Suppose it were NOT listed in `slotConfigNames`. What would production run after `staging` is swapped in?
hint: Without the mark, a setting is part of what moves with the content.

choices.text: The new version, paying into the test gateway
choices.why: An app setting that is not sticky travels with the content, so staging's value arrives in production with the new version.

choices.text: The new code with `SHOP_ENV=production`, because the gateway setting stays in its slot
choices.why: That is what a sticky setting does. An unmarked one moves.

choices.text: Nothing new: the swap refuses to start while the two values differ
choices.why: A swap does not compare settings before it starts; different values are the normal case.

choices.text: The old code, because a swap without sticky settings only exchanges them
choices.why: A swap always exchanges the content; settings are the part that may or may not go with it.

prompt: During a swap of `staging` into `production`, which of these stay with the production slot? Choose all that apply.
hint: What stays is the slot's identity: its addresses, who it is and what it may reach.

choices.text: Its custom domain names
choices.why: Custom domains are in the list of what is not swapped; production's address stays production's.

choices.text: An app setting with no sticky mark
choices.why: App settings follow the content unless they are listed as sticky.

choices.text: Its managed identity
choices.why: Managed identities stay with the slot, so the arriving code uses production's identity from the switch on.

choices.text: The image named in `linuxFxVersion`
choices.why: The image is the content; moving it is what the swap is for.

choices.text: A setting named in `slotConfigNames`
choices.why: That list is the declaration that a setting stays with its slot.

prompt: Match each command to what it does to the shop's app.
hint: One copies configuration, one marks it, one shares traffic and one undoes a pause.

pairs.left: `az webapp deployment slot create --slot staging --configuration-source shop-sp`
pairs.right: a new slot with production's settings and no content

pairs.left: `az webapp config appsettings set --slot staging --slot-settings SHOP_ENV=staging`
pairs.right: a setting that stays with its slot in a swap
a tenth of the visitors at production's address sent to staging

pairs.left: `az webapp deployment slot swap --slot staging --action reset`
pairs.right: a swap with preview cancelled, staging's settings put back

prompt: With the plan changed to `B1`, the shop's file still compiles with no warning, slot and all. Why did the compiler let it through?
hint: Where does the rule live, and where does the slot live?

choices.text: Basic allows one slot, so the file is valid as written
choices.why: The limits page lists no slots for Free or Basic; slots begin at Standard.

choices.text: Each resource is checked against its own type, and the tier rule spans two of them
choices.why: The plan's `sku` and the slot are separate resources; no type says a slot needs a plan of a certain tier, so Azure is the one that refuses.

choices.text: Child resources such as slots are not type-checked by Bicep
choices.why: The same compiler caught two mistakes in `slotConfigNames`, which is a child resource too.

choices.text: A slot on Basic is created stopped, which is a valid state
choices.why: Basic has no slots to create, stopped or running.

prompt: An app on a Premium v3 plan has eight deployment slots. To save money the team tries to move the plan to Standard. What happens?
hint: The slot count is a limit of the target tier, and the documentation says what it does to a scale-down.

choices.text: Standard has no slots, so all eight have to be deleted first
choices.why: Standard allows five slots per app; it is Free and Basic that have none.

choices.text: The newest three slots are deleted to fit, and the rest keep running
choices.why: App Service does not choose slots to delete for you; the change is refused instead.

choices.text: The change is refused until the app has five slots or fewer
choices.why: The documentation's own example: an app with more than five slots cannot scale down to Standard, which supports five.

choices.text: All eight keep running, but only five of them can be swapped
choices.why: There is no such half state; the tier's limit is on how many slots exist.

prompt: Put the steps of swapping `staging` into `production` in order.
hint: Everything until the switch happens to staging.
items: Apply production's sticky settings to every staging instance, which restarts them
Wait for every staging instance to finish restarting
Send a warm-up request to each staging instance
Switch the routing between the two slots
Restart the old content, now in staging, with staging's settings
trap: Switching the routing before the warm-up is exactly the downtime the swap exists to avoid.

prompt: The staging slot runs the slow-starting shop, which answers 503 on every path for its first seconds. No warm-up setting is configured. What does the swap's warm-up step do with the first 503?
hint: Read what the documentation says counts as warmed up when nothing is configured.

choices.text: Counts the instance as warm, since any HTTP response counts
choices.why: With no status list, an instance that returns any HTTP response is considered warmed up, and a 503 is a response.

choices.text: Waits up to 90 seconds for the root path to return 200
choices.why: The 90 seconds are how long it waits for an answer; with no list, any answer ends the wait.

choices.text: Stops the swap, because 503 is an error status
choices.why: A 503 stops the swap only when a status list exists and leaves 503 out.

choices.text: Asks five more times, then switches the routing whatever it heard
choices.why: The five retries are for requests that time out, and a 503 is not a timeout.

prompt: `WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_STATUSES` is `200`, and at the warm-up step one staging instance answers 503. What follows?
hint: Two different settings take a status list, and they react to a miss differently.

choices.text: The swap keeps asking that instance until it answers 200
choices.why: Asking again until a listed status arrives is what `WEBSITE_WARMUP_STATUSES` does at a container's start, not the swap's list.

choices.text: The routing switches, and the health check removes that instance afterwards
choices.why: The routing switches only when every instance is warm; a failed warm-up never reaches the switch.

choices.text: The swap stops, and production goes on serving the old version
choices.why: A status not in the list stops the warm-up and the swap, and production was never touched.

choices.text: Production is restarted so that the instance can be freed
choices.why: Nothing in a swap restarts production's instances before the switch.

prompt: The shop's plan is scaled to six instances and five of them fail the health check. `WEBSITE_HEALTHCHECK_MAXUNHEALTHYWORKERPERCENT` is at its default. How many instances are taken out of the load balancer?
hint: By default no more than half of the instances are excluded.

prompt: The team adds `autoSwapSlotName: 'production'` to the shop's staging slot, so that every push swaps itself in. The file compiles. What do they get?
hint: Check where the documentation says auto swap is supported, and what kind of app the shop is.

choices.text: Auto swap, once Always On is set on the slot
choices.why: Always On is already set in the file, and it is not the condition; the kind of app is.

choices.text: A swap on every push that skips the warm-up step
choices.why: Auto swap, where it exists, swaps after the warm-up; but the shop does not get it at all.

choices.text: Auto swap only after the plan moves to Premium
choices.why: The tier is not the obstacle; Standard and above have slots and swaps.

choices.text: Nothing: auto swap is unsupported for Linux and containers
choices.why: The documentation says auto swap is not supported in web apps on Linux or Web App for Containers, and the compiler cannot know which kind of app it is on.

prompt: Nobody orders from the shop between midnight and seven. Which of these costs nothing during those hours?
hint: Look for the one with a minimum of none.

choices.text: An App Service plan on Standard with autoscale down to one instance
choices.why: Autoscale moves the count, but a plan never has none; its last instance is billed all night.

choices.text: A Container App revision with a minimum of zero replicas, idle all night
choices.why: With no replicas running there is nothing to bill for usage, which is lesson 8's scale to zero.

choices.text: An AKS cluster on the Free tier with its nodes running
choices.why: The Free tier makes the control plane free; the nodes are virtual machines and are billed as such.

choices.text: A Premium v3 plan using automatic scaling
choices.why: Automatic scaling adds and removes instances on HTTP load, and keeps prewarmed ones besides; it does not reach zero.

prompt: The developers want to load-test staging without taking capacity from production. What does that cost them?
hint: Ask where a slot runs, and what a swap needs.

choices.text: Another plan, and with it the loss of the swap
choices.why: A slot runs on the plan's instances; separate machines mean a separate app, and a swap is between slots of one app.

choices.text: Nothing, since a staging slot runs on instances apart from production's
choices.why: A slot runs on the same instances as production, which is why a load test against it is a load test against production's machines.

choices.text: Turning off Always On in the staging slot during the test
choices.why: Always On keeps an app loaded; it does not move the slot's work to other machines.

choices.text: Marking the load test's settings as sticky
choices.why: Stickiness decides what moves in a swap, not where a slot's code runs.

prompt: Which of the shop's workloads is the wrong shape for an App Service plan?
hint: A plan bills its instances whether anything is happening or not.

choices.text: The order API, with customers through the day
choices.why: Steady traffic in one time zone is what a plan of fixed instances fits.

choices.text: The admin site the three developers use
choices.why: A small site sharing a plan already paid for costs only the capacity it takes.

choices.text: The nightly sales report, which runs ten minutes and exits
choices.why: A job that runs minutes a night would pay for a plan all day; a container group or a Container Apps job fits it.

choices.text: A customer-facing release once a week, tested first at a second address
choices.why: That is a slot and a swap, which is what the plan's Standard tier and above provide.

prompt: Which of these does App Service give the shop without the team building it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three are features of the platform; two belong to the other services.

choices.text: Slots, and a swap that warms the new version first
choices.why: Built into Standard and above, at no extra charge.

choices.text: Scale to zero on a dedicated tier at night
choices.why: A plan never has no instances; scale to zero is Container Apps, lesson 8.

choices.text: Custom domains with free managed certificates
choices.why: Managed certificates are listed from the Basic tier up.

choices.text: Built-in sign-in for the app's users
choices.why: App Service authentication is a platform feature, with nothing to write in the app.

choices.text: A Kubernetes API to install operators into
choices.why: There is no Kubernetes API on App Service; that is AKS, lesson 11.

prompt: The shop has split into five services that call each other; one scales on the length of a queue, and all of them are quiet at night. Where does it fit best?
hint: Weigh the idle row and how each service scales on its own events.

choices.text: One App Service plan carrying the five as apps
choices.why: They would share machines and scale together, with no scale on a queue of their own and the plan billed all night.

choices.text: Five container groups, one per service
choices.why: Container groups keep no count of copies and add none under load; scaling on a queue would be yours to build.

choices.text: Container Apps: five apps in one environment, each with its scale rule
choices.why: One network for the calls, a scale rule per app including a queue, and a minimum of zero for the quiet hours.

choices.text: AKS on the Free tier, because its control plane costs nothing
choices.why: The control plane is free there, but the nodes run and are billed through the night, and the cluster is the team's to operate.

prompt: What is the lowest App Service tier that has both deployment slots and autoscale?
hint: Both features begin at the same row of the limits table.

choices.text: Basic
choices.why: Basic has dedicated machines and manual scale-out, but no slots and no autoscale.

choices.text: Free
choices.why: Free runs on shared machines, with one instance and neither feature.

choices.text: Standard
choices.why: Standard is where five slots per app and autoscale both begin.

choices.text: Premium v3
choices.why: Premium v3 has both, and more slots, but it is not the lowest tier that does.

prompt: To run the new code in staging with production's settings, and stop there until somebody has tested it, run `az webapp deployment slot swap --slot staging --action ___`.
hint: The CLI's help names three actions: one starts the pause, one completes, one cancels.

prompt: Ten minutes after swapping `shop:1.1` into production, orders start failing. Nobody has deployed to staging since. What is the quickest way back?
hint: After a swap, where is the version production was running?

choices.text: Deploy `shop:1.0` to production again and wait for it to restart
choices.why: That restarts production in place, the break the slot exists to avoid, when the old version is already sitting warm in staging.

choices.text: Swap the same two slots again
choices.why: Staging holds the previous production content after the swap, so the same swap restores it, warmed, with production answering throughout.

choices.text: Send 100 percent of production's traffic to staging with traffic routing
choices.why: After the swap staging is the old version, so this works for visitors, but it leaves production's slot running the broken code and every pinned cookie to unwind.

choices.text: Run the swap with `--action reset`
choices.why: `reset` cancels a swap with preview that is still paused; this one finished ten minutes ago.

prompt: The shop's file points `WEBSITE_WARMUP_PATH`, `WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH` and `healthCheckPath` all at `/healthz`. What does that buy?
hint: Three readers, at three moments, asking one thing.

choices.text: App Service requires the three to name the same path
choices.why: Each has its own default and nothing requires them to agree; agreeing is a choice the file makes.

choices.text: The root path `/` is closed to platform requests, so another path is needed
choices.why: The default warm-up for a swap is `/` itself; nothing closes it.

choices.text: Start-up, swap and the check every minute all ask one question: is this instance ready to serve?
choices.why: One endpoint that answers 200 only when the shop is ready is read at container start, before the switch and every minute after it.

choices.text: It makes the health check skip instances that are still warming
choices.why: The health check asks every instance; an instance still warming answers 503 and counts as a failure until it is ready.
